The Los Angeles Times is read by people who wouldn’t mind running the country if they could find the time, and if they didn’t have to leave Southern California to do it. 6. The Boston Globe is read by people whose parents used to run the country and did a poor job of it, thank you very much. 7. 8. 9. 10. 11. 12. articles.text: The City Hall fountain is illuminated at night once again, showing its brand new tiles. The Piedmont Public Works Department has completed its project to replace tiles on the city’s two fountains – in front of City Hall and on the back side of the Exedra. The work included replacing existing tiling, adding tile to previously untiled vertical faces on the Exedra, replacing the lighting with energy efficient LEDs, and repairing lighting on the City Hall fountain that had not been illuminated in more than 10 years. The City Hall fountain was built in the mid 1980s. Originally untiled, tiles were added in the 1990s. The Exedra fountain and plaza was dedicated in honor of Piedmont resident Matthew Lempres in 2002. Both the City Hall and Exedra fountains had been in need of repair for several years – tiles were chipping and coming loose at an increasing pace. Every time the fountains were drained for cleaning, more tiles would need to be removed. Funding was included in the City’s budget for 2024 to retile both fountains. Pool tiles were used for the repairs since they are designed to be used underwater and are expected to be more durable than the previous tiles. The City Hall fountain restoration is complete. The Exedra fountain retiling is also complete, but Piedmont Public Works is awaiting delivery of a transformer before the fountain can be refilled with water. The Exedra fountain is being restored. articles.text: After holiday celebrations end, residents may dispose of their Christmas trees by using Republic Services curbside pickup or by cutting it up and placing it in a recycling cart. Holiday trees can quickly dry out and become a fire hazard. Once you are done with your tree, you should not leave it in your home or garage or lean it against your home outdoors. Curbside collection Curbside collection for natural trees is available December 26 through January 10. Republic Services will collect natural, unflocked trees until January 10. These trees will be turned into valuable compost and mulch. Put your tree out on your regular service day. Before placing your tree on the curb: • Remove everything from the tree: lights, decorations, tinsel, ornaments, and the tree stand. • If your tree is more than six feet tall, please cut it in half. Flocked or artificial trees Flocked, or “snow covered” trees are not compostable or recyclable. To dispose of a flocked or artificial tree, cut it up so that it fits in your black waste cart with the lid closed. Alternately, Republic Services will collect non-compostable trees curbside by request. Call 800-320-8077 to schedule a pickup: • There is a $33.33 disposal fee for curbside collection of non-compostable trees. • You can also use your annual Bulky Item Clean-ups for non-compostable trees in lieu of the pick-up fee. When placing non-compostable trees for curbside pickup, cut them into four foot or shorter pieces. For questions about holiday tree collection, email piedmont@ repsrv.com or call (800) 320-8077. articles.text: Gardens for a Changing Planet discussion on Jan. 15 Piedmont Garden Club welcomes the community to attend a discussion by Dr. Ari Novy, President and CEO of the San Diego Botanic Garden, on “Gardens for a Changing Planet: Towards a 21st Century Botanic Garden”. He will be the guest speaker on January 15 at 9:30 a.m. at Piedmont Community Hall. Botanic gardens are more than just beautiful public parks. They play important roles in plant science and conservation. Novy, an internationally recognized leader in the horticultural world, will show how botanic gardens are adapting as the climate changes, He will share how these important green spaces are the sites of research into medicinal, native, and food and agricultural plants. In addition to his role at the Garden, Novy is an active researcher, holding an appointment as Adjunct Associate Professor at Salk Institute for Biological Studies. He is the founding co-chair of the Food and Agriculture Professional Section of the American Public Gardens Association and has served on task forces and advisory panels for diverse groups including the White House Council on Environmental Quality, the Cornell Alliance for Science, Botanic Garden Conservation International, Rock Creek National Park, the Garden Club of America, the European and Mediterranean Plant Protection Organization, and many others. In 2024, he became an honorary member of the Garden Club of America. Piedmont Garden Club was founded in 1923 and has been a part of the Garden Club of America since 1926. Piedmont Garden Club members meet monthly to learn about garden-related topics including garden and floral design, garden photography, horticulture and environmental conservation. Other activities include hands-on workshops, field trips and work projects.

articles.text: With a CBS news crew at the South End Rowing Club on Sunday morning, December 14, it was a bit more lively than usual. But once we began our ritual it was a typical pre-winter morning. I keep my swim parka on to the last possible second, then we headed to the beach. The water is getting very cold now, bitter biting cold actually, and I had to force my breathing as I waded in. One big exhale and I was off. The first “2 minutes of misery” is really a test of resolve, and the only way to get through it is knowing that you’ll get used to it in a couple of minutes. Our pod headed west in the dark into a strong flood. I breathed on my left and kept watching the festive lights at Ghirardelli Square. As the first hint of light dawned in the east, we went under Muni Pier at Farnsworth Gap, and with a king tide we made it under without scraping any rocks or pilings – a painful hazard. Protected from the flood tide by Fort Mason pier, we cruised across the glassy channel and rendezvoused at the end of the pier. The Golden Gate was spectacular in the dawn’s early light. A couple of guys decided to head back from there while the rest of us pushed on to Gas House Cove against the flood. Adults, if you haven’t led a group of kids and young adults before, that’s okay. We can train you. Sea Scouts are recognized and rewarded for the things they learn and do. Scouts can earn certifications in SCUBA, boating safety, lifesaving, and CPR. Todd Sullivan resigns as boys’ soccer coach Following the winter of 2024, boys’ soccer head coach Todd Sullivan announced his resignation from his role after eight years, leaving Piedmont High after reviving the program. His teams finished on top of the Western Alameda County Conference Shoreline Division in 2019, 2021, and 2022, which earned them a promotion to the Foothill Division. Sullivan’s finest accomplishment was winning back-to-back Division 4 North Coast Section titles in 2022 and 2023. The first title came in a 1-0 win over No. 2 University as the No. 1 seed at Witter Field, while the second was another 1-nil win over No. 2 University, this time coming as the tournament’s Cinderella story as the No. 8 seed. The 2019 league title marked the school’s first in 10 years. That February night when Piedmont claimed the WACC banner appeared to be the turning point of the program. Sullivan signed on as head coach for the winter of 2016/2017, replacing Rory O’Connor, who in four years had only one NCS win and finished with a positive winning percentage just one time. PHS went 9-2-9 (W-T-L) in Sullivan’s first year and 7-2-13 his second year when still developing a system change—creating the high-pressing and possession style. He finished his time at Piedmont with 87 wins and 155 matches as head coach. He closes with a record of 87 wins, 19 ties, and 49 losses. Piedmont responded to a 6-5 deficit in the third quarter after allowing three consecutive goals, but the Highlanders won the day after a goal by Friedie Schickedanz and two by Ruby Guzdar. Holding the 8-7 lead, PHS consumed nearly three minutes of possession to win the game. It was a big game for goalie Annika Hattan-Kutter who recorded 12 saves. The Highlander season came to an end on May 2 at No. 4 Acalanes in Lafayette where they lost 9-7 in the D2 NCS Quarterfinals as the No. 5 seeded school. articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse’s newest production Waitress is playing onstage now through January 18. Susi Damilano’s revision of the motion picture Waitress, written by Adrienne Shelly, features music and lyrics by pop singer-songwriter Sara Bareilles. The play first premiered in 2015 at the American Repertory Theater in Cambridge, Massachusetts, and then transferred to Broadway in 2016, where it went on to receive 3 Tony Award nominations including Best Musical and Best Original Score. Waitress features protagonist Jenna, a diner waitress and expert pie maker, who is stuck in a small town and a loveless marriage. Jenna worries she will have to abandon her dream of opening her own bakery when she becomes unexpectedly pregnant, until she enters a baking contest and meets the soon-to-be love of her life. Ruby Day plays Jenna, and is supported by Zeke Edmonds, who plays Jenna’s love interest Dr. Pomatter. Supporting characters include Louis Parnell, Dorian Lockett, Tanika Baptiste and Sharon Shao. Music Direction is by Dave Dobrusky and choreography by Nicole Helfer. Waitress is playing at San Francisco Playhouse through January 18, 2025. The venue is located at 450 Post Street in the heart of San Francisco’s Union Square theatre district. The show is on stage six days a week, Tuesday through Sunday. articles.text: A patron views the Mary Cassatt at Work exhibit at the Legion of Honor. An exhibition featuring the work of Impressionist painter Mary Cassatt is on view at the Legion of Honor in San Francisco through January 26. Mary Cassatt at Work is the first North American retrospective of Cassatt’s work in 25 years. The exhibition, which includes 93 objects on loan from institutions including the National Gallery of Art, Washington, DC, the Philadelphia Museum of Art, and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston, focuses on the roles of women and children in the late 19th century. Cassatt’s paintings often depict ‘women’s work,’ including knitting and needlepoint, bathing children and nursing infants. “Mary Cassatt at Work disrupts any preconceived notion that Cassatt was a sentimental painter and sheds fresh light on her groundbreaking practice,” said Thomas Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “It is fitting that this exhibition, which celebrates Cassatt’s daring and modernity, will open our yearlong centennial celebration of the Legion of Honor. The Legion of Honor was cofounded in 1924 by another intrepid female pioneer, Alma de Bretteville Spreckels, who shared Cassatt’s deep attachment to French culture and bold vision for the future of art in America,” Campbell said. The exhibition presents a group of distinguished works, including Cassatt’s magisterial oil portrait of her mother and recently acquired pastels from the Fine Arts Museums’ collection. Organizing curator Emily Beeny said the mother-and-child theme was to Cassatt’s final decades what water lilies were to Monet’s or apples to Cézanne’s. “Because this motif is and was so freighted with gendered meaning, it’s been too easy to write these pictures off as sweet or sentimental, when in fact they’re formally rigorous, engaged in an ever-deepening conversation with tradition and an ever more experimental handling of paint,” Beeny said. “Given the social realities of Cassatt’s time, it’s perhaps useful to reflect on the fact that these works are all, in some sense, brought to us by Cassatt’s own childless state. The ambition and scope of her career were, alas, quite incompatible in the late 19th century with marriage and childbearing, even for a woman of her elevated social class.” Visit https://www.famsf. org/exhibitions/mary-cassatt?mc_cid=f4db3a4148&mc_ eid=573801a180 to learn more and to purchase tickets to the museum.

articles.text: Meet the artist on Jan. 6 Bermuda-born artist Soleé Darrell’s solo exhibition Cosmic Ceremony is on display at the Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco now through February 2. The artist said that being from Bermuda and living in the United States has given her the unique perspective of embracing multiple identities. Darrell, now based in Northern California, creates silk velvet paintings that explore color, sound, and texture as tools for healing and self-discovery. The exhibition features seven paintings and a single sculpture using various mediums, but most frequently delicate silk. Her paintings often mimic galaxies, star formations, and supernovae. Darell’s new works displayed at MoAD, including Within the body are gardens (2024) and Blessed are they who remember (2024). They are organic forms that blend free-flowing colors, while her large-scale sculpture Ritual is all we have (2024) uses silk velvet, boat rope, velvet ribbon, and found trimmings to create a nearly-symmetrical form in clashing pigments. Visit the museum on Monday, January 6 at 6:30 p.m. for a conversation and reception with Darrell, an Emerging Artist Program awardee. She will be in conversation with Oakland artist Angela Hennessy. articles.text: Treasure Island Museum will host a panel discussion on Yerba Buena Island’s natural history. On Saturday, January 11 at 10 a.m. It is free to the public. Yerba Buena Island is the second largest natural island in San Francisco Bay, and its development and restoration is an on-going and multi-phase effort, much like the larger, man-made Treasure Island. Yerba Buena Island was historically used as a naval base and training center and its native ecosystems have been replaced by invasive species. Significant and biodiverse natural areas still remain, and ongoing redevelopment of Yerba Buena Island and Treasure Island provided the opportunity to restore native ecology. Both islands have been planted with mor than 50 species of native plants, including flora and fauna that are native to the ecosystem. According to Treasure Island Museum staff, the design and planning for these spaces involved a unique and collaborative effort between developers, the City of San Francisco, ecologists, local nurseries and landscape architects. Peter Brastow, from the San Francisco Environment Department and Will Benge, Senior Associate with CMG Landscape Architecture will lead a discussion of restoration efforts. Tickets are free, but reservations are required. Visit https:// www.treasureislandmuseum.org/ event-details/restoration-of-yerba-buena-island-weaving-ecology-with-place-and-infrastructure to register. View from Yerba Buena Island

articles.text: Visit historic Filoli House and Garden in Woodside now through January 12 to see the 16-acre estate decorated for the holidays. Filoli’s team has installed and decorated 22 trees, 3,600 light strands that stretch more than 18 miles, with more than 7,000 luminescent ornaments, and 1,000 feet of festive garlands. The Reception Room’s 18-foot ceiling create an appropriate location for “The Grand Tree,” the tallest tree on display. The two-story historic mansion contains 56 rooms, including a ballroom and reception room designed to host concerts and debutante balls. Each room in the mansion is adorned with holiday decorations that complement the room’s original hues and aesthetics. The design team carefully recreated the original holiday placement used by Agnes and William Bourn, Filoli’s first owners. Original artifacts can be viewed throughout the home. Lurline Roth, who lived with her family in the mansion after the Bourns, was an avid collector of religious icons. Her Italian Murano glass nativity scene is now on display in the study. While holiday evenings at Filoli are truly a sight to see, the lighting enhancements glow just as festively during the day. Daytime admission allows visitors to explore the estate trail before sundown and admire the garden’s autumnal colors. Daytime hours are 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. The estate is open until 9 p.m. through January. To learn more about holidays at Filoli and to purchase tickets, visit https://filoli.org/events/holidays/.

articles.text: After reflecting on the year past, my sense is that if the mood of the country were a weather report I would judge it to be overcast, dark clouds on the horizon, often stormy. To continue the metaphor, at times it can feel like trying to fly a kite in a hurricane of cynicism. As an antidote to 2024, or as a reminding that decency and good will are still embedded in our culture, I would recommend three films: Frank Capra’s It’s a Wonderful Life, Nora Ephron’s Sleepless in Seattle, and The Simple Life of Noah Dearborn (all streaming). Each is an extraordinary example of the ability of movies to remind us of who we are or wish to be, all while using the wondrous confluence of imagery, dialogue and sound track. It’s a Wonderful Life, is set in Bedford Falls, NY, the year is 1928. It focuses on George Bailey (James Stewart), first as a boy, then as a young man who is filled with dreams of leaving his small town behind and traveling to exotic places worldwide that only he can imagine. But circumstances – his sense of duty and commitment, his innate decency, and, of course, love - redefine George’s dreams while years slip away (the Great Depression followed by WWII). This heartfelt story is told through the prism of director Frank Capra who demonstrates a belief in the inherent integrity and goodness of people, qualities often lost in many of our more contemporary films. Rated PG. 2hrs 9min Sleepless in Seattle, at least initially, is framed by grief and loss. Written and directed by Nora Ephron, who turns the profound sadness of a young architect, Sam Baldwin (Tom Hanks), and his 10-year-old son Jonah (Ross Malinger), into a compelling story, set in Seattle, someJames Stewart in It’s a Wonderful Life Sidney Poitier and Mary-Louise Parker in The Simple Life of Noah Dearborn Meg Ryan and Tom Hanks in Sleepless in Seattle time in the 1990s. Sleepless is actually two parallel stories, one involving a young journalist, Annie Reed (Meg Ryan), recently engaged to Walter (Bill Pullman). Unexpectedly, she finds herself redefining her dreams of what love should be, while wondering if her relationship with Walter truly touches her heart. This nudging doubt is revealed one night as she is driving to her home in Baltimore. While listening to talk radio, a call-in show hosted by psychologist Dr. Marcia, she hears Jonah telling the “shrink” about his dad, Sam, who deeply misses his wife, as Jonah feels the absence of his mother. This moment, with Jonah’s voice filling the darkness, is the sweet spot of the narrative, and is slowly revealed and embellished in scene after remarkable scene (some moving and others comedic). We soon come to realize that Sleepless is a love story though Sam and Annie never meet until that much anticipated encounter on top of the Empire State Building takes place on St. Valentine’s Day. Of course, this occurs with the help of Jonah. And not to forget the recurring reference to the 1940s film An Affair to Remember. A brief comment about the Sleepless soundtrack: it is so good. The song choices made by Norah Ephron are inspired, and help tell the story, opening with the voice of Jimmy Durante (actor/comedian from the 1940s). Sleepless in Seattle. articles.text: There were many reasons for the Walking on Wednesday group to be at Exedra last Wednesday. The group walks every Wednesday, rain or shine, but it was Christmas and Hanukkah. The last time the holidays were on the same day was in 2005. It won’t happen again until 2035. It was also the last Wednesday of the year, so there was a good turnout of 19 walkers and one K-9 best friend to celebrate this special morning together. The group was mindful of the services provided by the Piedmont Police and Fire Departments, and especially appreciative of the people who were on duty this holiday morning. The walkers went to the police station where they met officer Hugo Diaz, then next door to the fire station where they met firefighters Chad Walker, Brittany Burges, and Lucas Romero. Both the police and fire personnel were thankful for the group’s gift of donuts. After the visits the group was off to see the homes in the central part of Piedmont that are decorated with representations of the 12 Days of Christmas gifts. As a holiday tradition, some residents of Highland, Caperton, and Sheridan Avenues display the items of the 12 Days of Christmas carol in their windows or entryways. It was shared that 12 Days of Christmas is an English Christmas carol, however it may have also been a catechism song for young Catholics during the 16th through early 19th Centuries. During this period Roman Catholics in England were not permitted to practice their faith openly. Someone may have written this carol with two levels of meaning. One is the surface meaning, but the other may have been known only to Church members. Each gift in the carol may have been a code for a Catholic religious concept which the children could remember. The walkers went down Guilford looking for decorated houses. They didn’t find any, but on Highland they soon found a partridge in a sparkling pear tree in a front window. The walkers continued, finding two turtle doves, three French hens (drawn by the family’s s three children), and four calling birds. The group turned up Caperton Avenue and found five golden rings, six geese a-laying, and ten lords a-leaping. They arrived at Sheridan Avenue searching for eleven pipers piping and twelve drummers drumming. Going back towards Highland, they found them in two more windows. The group’s search and walk were complete. It was time for them to wrap up 2024 and go home to continue their holidays. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register at https://tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. On hand for last week’s walk on Wednesday were Albert Chen, Vicki Trimbach, Sherona and Jack Fischrup with K-9 best friend Kojak, Phil Witte, Elizabeth Richter, Denny McGee, Peggy and Dana Shultz, Pat and Greg Keller, Sherry Jacobs, Bonnie Sherwood, Mark Davis, Dick and Mary Carter, Irene Thompson, Jim Kuo, and Marianne Jakus.

articles.text: Photo by Deborah Quok Greek-Inspired Longevity Bean Soup is a great dish for a cold winter day. Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on January 4, 2024. It is never too soon to be proactive about your health and longevity. As we ring in the New Year, many of us have considered that healthy lifestyle goals and the meals we consume are a large part of it. Gigantic Royal Corona beans are the stars of this soup. They cook up tender and, dare I say, “meaty” owing to their size and toothsomeness. They’re as fun to eat as they are impressive to those new to them. Greek-Inspired Longevity Bean Soup Adapted from Diane Kochilas’ Fasolada – Bean Soup with Pumpkin & Corn Makes about 3 quarts INGREDIENTS • 1/2 pound giant beans such as Royal Corona or Greek gigantes • 1/4 cup extra-virgin olive oil, divided, preferably Greek • 1-1/2 red onion, coarsely chopped, about 1-1/2 cups • 2 tablespoons fresh garlic, minced, divided • 1 tablespoon tomato paste • 1 14.5 ounce can diced tomatoes • 1 bay leaf • 1/2 teaspoon dried oregano, or 2 sprigs fresh • 1 3-inch-long strip of fresh orange peel • 1 cup corn kernels • 1 cup cubed delicata or butternut squash • 1/4 cup fresh flat-leaf parsley, roughly chopped • 1 – 2 teaspoons honey, preferably local • 1 tablespoon balsamic vinegar, scant measure to taste • 1/2 – 1 teaspoon sea salt, to taste • A few grinds black peppercorns, to taste INSTRUCTIONS Check the beans for debris, rinse and then soak overnight; drain and discard the soaking water. Soaking is optional but will decrease the cooking time considerably. Heat 2 tablespoons olive oil in a large soup pot over medium heat. Add the red onion and cook until soft and translucent, about 5–10 minutes. Stir occasionally to prevent scorching. Stir in 1 tablespoon of the minced garlic (set remaining 1 tablespoon aside for later), give it a quick stir; then add the tomato paste. Stir again to incorporate the tomato paste well. Add the drained beans, canned tomatoes, bay leaf, oregano, and orange peel. Top off with enough water to cover by 2 inches. Bring to a boil then reduce to a simmer until the beans are very tender, about 1-1/2 to 2 hours. When the beans are tender, scoop out about 1 cup of the soup and puree in a food processor or blender/immersion stick blender, then return to the pot. This blending step is optional but will add a bit of body to the soup. Meanwhile, heat the remaining 2 tablespoons of olive oil in a large skillet over medium heat. Cook the squash and corn until lightly browned, then add the remaining garlic and sea salt. Mix well then add to the soup pot once the beans have cooked through and the pureed portion has been added back to the pot. Return the soup to a simmer and adjust the seasoning with additional salt and black pepper. Just before serving remove the orange peel and bay leaf. Stir in the chopped parsley, honey and balsamic vinegar. Serve with an additional drizzle of high-quality, extra-virgin olive oil and a few sprinkles of parsley. For additional information and to search more recipes, see the blog of Piedmont resident Deborah Quok at: https://www. piedmontpantry.com/.

articles.text: These concept sketches were made by Mark Becker, in the very early stages of his design for Piedmont’s Havens Elementary School. Certainly not all details are (yet) shown, but these rough drawings can be considered the blueprint for all the design and construction work that was to follow for this wonderful job. This column appeared in the Post originally on August 3, 2022. As a tribute to the late Will Adams, it is being reprinted. It was his 49th column in his biweekly observations and comments on the architecture of Piedmont with examples with photos and sketches from around the world. Will Adams was a talented Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who lived in Piedmont for 30 years. All good designs have at their source a strong, clear vision, or concept. This can be defined as the overall main idea – a view into the future of what the project should look like, feel like and how it will function. The built environment around us – the places we work, live, play and interact with each other – is in reality an ongoing design process that has an important effect on all of our lives, often much more than we realize. As we must continually upgrade, accommodate, and adapt to the new, this process especially requires a strong vision. Walking around Piedmont and looking at the various finished buildings, landscapes, urban designs and planning decisions at various different scales, it is instructive to judge how clear the initial visions were, and how well they were adhered to during the often lengthy design and construction processes. It makes us ask how strong will be our evolving city vision(s) going forward in the next months, years and decades? Inspiration for concept direction in the built environment can be derived from many sources, such as the local architectural history of a place, the logical transportation connections, the solar orientation, a response to a dramatic view, or surrounding existing geographical features. Vision can also be inspired by a need for change, an opportunity to accommodate current needs by adjusting existing patterns to enhance function, aesthetics and/ or to build and strengthen the community. In most cases there are a number of considerations, sometimes competing, that make up a vision. For effective implementation, the best concepts and resulting designs will have a clear hierarchy of importance assigned to each of their parts. It is a way to prevent small or unimportant aspects from controlling the big picture and compromising the vision. This somewhat more developed, more detailed concept drawing was made to provide an upgraded vision statement for a multifamily island housing boating community in the Caribbean.

pages.text: Thursday, January 2, 2025 25 The importance of vision for the built environment Vision statements in environmental design can be thought of and used in much the same way artists attach theme sketches or photos to their easels: to provide a constant reminder and reference to an overall concept during the course of the work. Communicating a vision is essential for success. It should be clear enough to be stated, drawn or written. I used to have as a client Jim Thompson, who ran Vail Resorts. He astutely insisted that with any project, the concept and goal should be able to be stated in one concise sentence. He was absolutely right! Not only does this clarify the idea, but it also makes it easier for everyone concerned to continually evaluate the design and construction process for adherence to the stated purpose. As the number of participants associated with a project grows as it progresses, it is easy to confuse, forget, or dilute the primary concept. One of the principal tasks of the design professions, the owners, as well as the concerned public should be guarding and protecting the main vision of a project through all phases to completion. These concept sketches were made by Mark Becker, in the very early stages of his design for Piedmont’s Havens Elementary School. Certainly not all details are (yet) shown, but these rough drawings can be considered the blueprint for all the design and construction work that was to follow for this wonderful job. By Will Adams This column appeared in the Post originally on August 3, 2022. As a tribute to the late Will Adams, it is being reprinted. It was his 49th column in his biweekly observations and comments on the architecture of Piedmont with examples with photos and sketches from around the world. Will Adams was a talented Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who lived in Piedmont for 30 years. All good designs have at their source a strong, clear vision, or concept. This can be defined as the overall main idea – a view into the future of what the project should look like, feel like and how it will function. The built environment around us – the places we work, live, play and interact with each other – is in reality an ongoing design process that has an important effect on all of our lives, often much more than we realize. As we must continually upgrade, accommodate, and adapt to the new, this process especially requires a strong vision. Walking around Piedmont and looking at the various finished buildings, landscapes, urban designs and planning decisions at various different scales, it is instructive to judge how clear the initial visions were, and how well they were adhered to during the often lengthy design and construction processes. It makes us ask how strong will be our evolving city vision(s) going forward in the next months, years and decades? Inspiration for concept direction in the built environment can be derived from many sources, such as the local architectural history of a place, the logical transportation connections, the solar orientation, a response to a dramatic view, or surrounding existing geographical features. Vision can also be inspired by a need for change, an opportunity to accommodate current needs by adjusting existing patterns to enhance function, aesthetics and/ or to build and strengthen the community. In most cases there are a number of considerations, sometimes competing, that make up a vision. For effective implementation, the best concepts and resulting designs will have a clear hierarchy of importance assigned to each of their parts. It is a way to prevent small or unimportant aspects from controlling the big picture and compromising the vision. This somewhat more developed, more detailed concept drawing was made to provide an upgraded vision statement for a multifamily island housing boating community in the Caribbean. However abstract a concept sketch is, the main theme should be immediately clear. In the first example it is respecting the view corridors represented by the yellow arrows, and the dominance of the pedestrian street pattern for development in Vail, Colorado.

articles.text: With profound sadness, the family of Harvey Anderson has confirmed his sudden passing on December 19, 2024 at the age of 61. Harvey James Anderson II was a proud father and husband, an accomplished lawyer, a dedicated sponsor and mentor, a cherished friend and an avid surfer, who led his life with love and light. Born in Washington, DC, Harvey was raised by his parents, Joan and Harvey. Andersson, who instilled in him a strong sense of family, community, and faith that guided him throughout his adult life and career. Harvey progressively followed a call west starting with Milwaukee, Wisconsin where he completed his Bachelor’s Degree in Engineering at Marquette University and built friendships that would prove to be lifelong. Upon graduation, he continued on his westward path, finally settling by the ocean he loved so deeply in the San Francisco Bay Area, which he called home for more than 35 years. There, he studied law at the University of San Francisco School of Law, which set him on course for a prolific career, throughout which he was known and admired for his strategic vision and commitment to doing the right thing. His work ethic and talent brought him to the most senior offices at the intersection of tech, law, and policy. He led the legal and policy functions at HP as the Chief Legal Officer, successfully navigated the business, legal and policy needs of AVG, and used his innovative thinking to create some of the most impactful policy and business programs at Mozilla. After retirement, Harvey dedicated himself to beginning a new adventure as an Adjunct Professor at University of California Berkeley School of Law on the “business of law.” He served on the Board of Trustees for Marquette University, was a member of the board of Common Sense Media, and was a strategic advisor and board member for startups throughout his career. Less formally, he always freely and enthusiastically gave wisdom and advice to anyone who sought him out for mentorship or career guidance - even if his sons sometimes gave him feedback that his lessons took too long. His intellect, judiciousness, and talent as a leader and lawyer made him an incredible force in the workplace but his greatest gifts to the world were his spirit of warmth, generosity, and devoHarvey Anderson died suddenly on December 9 at age 61. tion to his family and community. As someone guided deeply by his faith, Harvey was committed to service and driven by a sense of responsibility to share the goodness that life bestowed upon him with others. He found every opportunity to give to those in need, either donating time at local organizations, building houses annually for underserved communities in Mexico, or even just being an available ear to listen and support as someone who battled life’s challenges. Harvey proudly achieved 35 years of sobriety through hard work, dedication and support from members of the Program. His commitment to the Program was unmatched as he served as a guiding light and sponsor to countless men and women, supporting their journeys to not only reach sobriety, but to thrive. Harvey had a rare gift to make someone feel seen, heard, and understood. But Harvey was at his happiest when spending time with his wife, Denelle, and their five sons, Luke, Cole, Dylan, Trevor, and Jax. Harvey and Denelle’s journey to each other took time, but when they found each other and blended their families, Harvey embraced every moment spent together and lived his most core values to ensure their home was joyful, supportive, and welcoming. He was there to cheer them on at events whether sports performances or, in Denelle’s case, speaking engagements (for which he had a front row seat for her speeches from Rome to Nairobi), He was there to play any and all games together from board games and trivia to pickleball and paintball, to spend holidays in their favorite places always trying to get to surfing (especially Hawaii), or just quiet time together. His family was the center of his world and he was immensely proud of his wife and sons. Harvey will be remembered for always saying yes to life – yes to fun, yes to sharing his good fortune, yes to anything with his boys and wife, yes to putting his feet in the ocean, yes to discovering the world, yes to listening, yes to being there for those who asked or needed him – and always yes to surfing. Harvey was the embodiment of someone who lived his life to the fullest and in service of those he loved and his community. In doing so, he managed to touch so many lives, inspiring each one to carry on his legacy. He leaves behind his loving family, mother Joan Fowler Anderson, wife Denelle Dixon, and their sons Cole Anderson, Luke Anderson, Dylan Thayer, Trevor Thayer, and Jax Thayer. He is predeceased by his father Harvey James Anderson A memorial service will be held at Corpus Christi Church in Piedmont, on January 9, 2025 at 7:00 pm. A celebration of Harvey’s tremendous life will be held on January 11. In lieu of flowers, the family requests that memorial donations be made to: Marquette University (https://www.givecampus.com/campaigns/28093/ donations/new?a=9077221), and Surfrider Foundation (https:// www.surfrider.org/?form=memorial).

Retracing our steps when we have misplaced Jesus Luke bridges the story of Jesus birth with the story of the journey Jesus’ family took to Jerusalem when he was twelve years old. There, they misplaced him. They were well on their way home before they realized he was not with them. They then retraced their steps and found him still in Temple, discussing important matters with the leading teachers of the day. Once again, we do well to follow the example of Jesus’ parents. Life gets busy. We lose focus. Despite our best intentions, we misplace Jesus. When this happens, we do well to go back to where we saw him last. This could be the manger. It could be the Temple. It could be the cross. It could be the garden outside the empty Tomb. Fortunately, when we misplace Jesus, we have some reliable places to return to. even as we journey into 2025. Rev. Jim Hopkins is senior Pastor of Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church, Lakeshore Avenue and Mandana Boulevard, Oakland. And so the story develops, filled with charming moments and an outstanding performance by Dianne Wiest. She was nominated for an Emmy for Best Supporting Actress, delivering a superb portrayal of Sarah McClelland, a neighbor who lives just down the road from Noah and constantly searches for reasons to have him repair something while thanking him with a homemade pie. And, of course, there’s Sidney Poitier who will be deeply missed. The Simple Life of Noah Dearborn. Directed by Greg Champion. Released in 1999. Streaming on Fandango/Prime/ Apple tv. Each replaces cynicism with hope, buttressed by kindness, each a gift of sorts to reflect upon as we go forward into 2025. Best wishes.

articles.text: Piedmont residents voted on new City Council members in 2024, electing Conna McCarthy to a second term on the Council and welcoming new Council member Lorrel Plimier. Betsy Andersen was named the city’s new mayor succeeding Jen Cavenaugh who served two terms on City Council. Piedmont voters approved Conna McCarthy for a second 4-year term on City Council and confirmed Lorrel Plimier as a new member of the council. McCarthy won 4,799 votes and Plimier won 3,605 votes, placing them at 43.43% and 32.62% of the vote respectively. Plimier was sworn into office on December 16 to join four other members of Piedmont’s City Council, and McCarthy was confirmed for a second four-year term. The special city council meeting took place in the Community Hall and included the swearing in of three new school board members.
